errands and meetings, so another short, informal post.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Donald Trump will never admit that his gratuitous Iran war has been a total disaster. But the debacle has clearly broken him. So we are now saddled with a president who has given up governing, but will maintain his grip on power wherever he can. And his power will be exclusively focused on rage and revenge.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hence Trump has appointed Bill Pulte as the acting Director of National Intelligence (DNI), a position critical to national security.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The word “acting” is crucial. The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/539d1861-7f74-4bf7-a530-d25cafc8c70b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">statute</a><span> creating the position of DNI explicitly requires that the appointee “shall have extensive national security expertise.” Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, has no background in anything related to national security. So Trump is trying to bypass a Congressional confirmation process that would put Pulte under the spotlight. Even Republicans might shed their slavish obedience at this point, given Trump’s plummeting poll numbers and his betrayal of John Cornyn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But pointing out that Pulte is unqualified for his new job doesn’t convey the extent to which Trump is trolling America with this new appointment.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For Pulte isn’t merely unqualified for a sensitive national security position. He’s unqualified, intellectually and morally, for </span><em>any</em><span> government position. All he has are the qualifications that matter to Trump: he is a shameless lackey and willing hitman for Trump’s vendettas.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Who is Pulte? He’s a wealthy nepo-baby, the grandson of the founder of PulteGroup, the nation’s third-largest residential builder. He likes to present himself as the face of the family business, but as a devastating </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1d465050-472a-4b8f-ab1b-821b5fbd1df7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">New York Times profile</a><span> last year explained, he was pushed off PulteGroup’s board in 2020. The family’s charitable foundation has issued a statement that “Bill Pulte does not represent, nor is he a spokesperson for, all members of the Pulte family, in any capacity.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Times goes on to note that</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These days, one of Bill Pulte’s primary connections to the residential real estate business is a group of five aging mobile home parks he owns in Florida, some badly in need of repair.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">How has Pulte handled his falling out with his family?</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Mr. Pulte has spent years battling with his aunt, the foundation’s president, over his grandfather’s legacy and other issues. In social media posts he has called her “totally fake and phony” and has written that she “defecates” about him and his late grandfather’s legacy on the foundation website.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thousands of nasty political posts on social media landed Pulte a powerful post in the Trump administration. And while his former role in his family’s business may have led to his appointment as director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, his real job has been weaponizing the agency as a tool against Trump’s perceived enemies — weaponization that is being investigated by the Government Accountability Office as a potential </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0c6f08e-8012-47e0-8dbf-d4624d54c3a9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">misuse of authority</a><span>. Pulte confected </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cd3fd293-6228-4240-bf1f-c5ada06df918?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">false claims</a><span> of mortgage fraud to try to push out Lisa Cook, the only black woman on the Federal Reserve Board. He has leveled similar trumped-up charges against Letitia James, New York’s Attorney General, and several Democratic politicians. And he pushed groundless fraud accusations against Jerome Powell, the former Federal Reserve chair, who stood in the way of Trump’s attempt to politicize monetary policy.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Pulte is a bumbling hatchet man: so far none of his attempted lynchings have succeeded. But for Trump, willingness to engage in unethical behavior is all that matters.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What will Pulte do as America’s senior intelligence official? You might think that even someone like Trump, who has no desire to serve the national interest, who sees wars only as ways to enrich himself and distract from his domestic woes, would want accurate intelligence. After all, if you’re going to wag the dog, you don’t want the dog to bite back the way it has in Iran.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Trump appears to have given up on governing — even governing aimed at consolidating his own power and legacy. He wants to punish everyone he imagines has wronged him but has lost all interest in making the government work, even for nefarious purposes. So he don’t need no intelligence, just someone who will indulge his rage. And that will be Pulte’s job.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Just to be clear, I am by no means saying that Trump’s descent into rage-madness has ended the threat to U.S. democracy. The Koch-backed Federalist Society, which now controls the Supreme Court, is going all in on rigging U.S. elections with the goal of locking in permanent Republican rule. The architects of Project 2025 are marching ahead with their goal of turning the federal government into a spoils system that answers only to billionaires and their political pawns. Politicization of research funding is getting very close to destroying a scientific community that took generations to build.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Trump himself is, at this point, little more than a festering ball of anger and hate.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/8f0607e2-1db2-45ba-8116-54d45e6f6517?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/KmbCOMM8peo" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/da3244ad-fa4b-4ce3-87b6-5c53cf40c652?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">NurPhoto</a><span>/Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A debate has been raging on the internet between Paul Krugman (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0623b7c-b4fd-476d-b9d9-1c1f7a3f3fcd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ad8e3409-c0fe-4a15-95ca-68956899eae5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>, and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0f858f34-91e5-4b7f-9f67-0852e60e495f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">here</a><span>) and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/52b809f8-d201-46bb-953d-3225f5ac0376?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">three European economists</a><span> — Philippe Aghion, Antonin Bergeaud, and Luis Garicano — in which Krugman maintains that the conventional wisdom that America’s productivity has risen faster than Europe’s is mistaken. This all hinges on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8d35168d-e732-4324-81ae-445602e4a7fb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">technical issues</a><span> about the construction of purchasing power parities, but the debate is being waged with a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/750d25d6-9c68-4e1f-b475-b88a8d4e7970?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">level of emotionality and vehemence</a><span> that suggests something more.   </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nobody is quite saying it explicitly, but I think that Americans like to argue about “Europe” (a construct that of course flattens major differences between countries) primarily because it’s actually an argument about the United States. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a sense that progressive Americans want to make our country more “like Europe” and that therefore if Europe is bad that says bad things about the progressive project, whereas if Europe is good that says good things about the project. Of course this involves huge handwaving oversimplifications, but I do think it basically captures what’s going on here. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Much of the territory this debate covers is well trod. But I realized it might be interesting to consider it from the perspective of a country that is almost universally seen as an economic success story: Poland. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Poland was poorer than Western Europe dating back to well before World War II, and it then suffered for decades under Communist economic mismanagement and domination by the Soviet Union. But since the fall of the Berlin Wall, Poland has done extremely well. It’s not that Poland is suddenly the richest country in the world, but it’s growing </span><em>more rapidly</em><span> than the U.S., catching up to the global frontier, and threatening to soon leave stagnating countries like Italy and the United Kingdom in the dust. </span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure interesting development success story in part because it became rich through a model that always seemed like it should work according to a textbook but that in practice people rarely if ever saw. In fact, until recent years, it had become a bit of conventional wisdom that you actually </span><em>couldn’t</em><span> grow as rich as Poland has this way. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Poland is also interesting because it poses the question of what are the stakes in this discourse exactly? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Conservatives are normally happy to acknowledge Poland as a success. The chart above tells an “up from Communism” kind of story, pregnant with implications for how prosperous Cuba might become if it ditched a failed economic model and embraced economic integration with the enormous and very rich country directly to its north. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And yet, insofar as “Europe” means anything in public policy terms, I think Poland definitely counts as part of “Europe.” Not just geographically, but in the sense that the main elements of the social model that American progressives like are present there. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Poland’s growth model</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But first, the part of this story that I find most interesting. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Poland’s economic growth has been driven largely by foreign direct investment. That’s a striking contrast to the growth model Joe Studwell and Ha-Joon Chang have touted in their books looking primarily at the success of Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and mainland China. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The story they told about Asian growth is that a naive belief in establishing sound economic fundamentals isn’t enough. Economic-development success stories, on this view, require you to develop home-grown companies. Openness to investment and general embrace of capitalism are part of the story, but you also need a lot of “industrial policy” bells and whistles to grow your own Samsung, Toyota, TSMC, or BYD. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But while there are obviously Polish companies in Poland, they aren’t really global success stories. The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38e1a1f4-33b8-4445-8043-070059a286b9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">six biggest Polish companies by revenue</a><span> all have the Polish state as their largest shareholder. Three of them are electric utilities, one is an oil company, and one is a lottery that seems to have expanded into other gambling pursuits. Then there’s KGHM, which seems to be a real mining conglomerate with global operations. The seventh biggest company, Dino, is a supermarket chain. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Which is just to say there is no Polish manufacturing champion out there crushing it in global export markets. But even without big, famous Polish manufacturing companies, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/02e3bf6d-cb09-4c35-9367-8be3017993b8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the country has a thriving export sector</a><span> with Polish-made cars and car parts, computers, gas turbines, monitors, and batteries sold on world markets.  </span></p><div Complexity</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So what’s the deal? Well, foreign companies — especially, though not exclusively, German ones — invested a lot of money in setting up factories in Poland. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In turn, fully </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/02e3bf6d-cb09-4c35-9367-8be3017993b8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">a quarter</a><span> of Polish exports go to Germany. A lot of German companies partially offloaded their supply chains to Poland, where labor is cheaper, taking advantage of Polish membership in the European Union to make things seamless. And the Polish government has welcomed foreign investment by setting up special export zones even before E.U. accession and being open to investment from countries other than Germany as well. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Investors seem to have a lot of confidence that Poland is not going to expropriate their stuff or discriminate against foreign companies to advantage politically connected locals, so Poland just keeps converging with richer European countries. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An optimist might have hoped this would work for Mexico in the wake of NAFTA. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But even though Mexico </span><em>has</em><span> attracted a lot of American investment and has some successful export sectors, the Mexican economy as a whole has not done very well. The basic story people tell about this is that Mexico has become bifurcated between a relatively small export-oriented formal sector and a much larger economy of locally facing service companies that have very low productivity and little growth and prevent the dynamic export sector from driving broader prosperity. This is all connected to the infamous problem of drug cartels, massive corruption, and high levels of violence. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Even more prosperous places have some version of this dual economy: High tech drives the economy of the Bay Area, but way more people work in restaurants or health care than in tech. Globally traded exports are just not that labor-intensive. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Poland, unlike Mexico, has a basically functioning state with the rule of law, so the benefits of its growing export sector spread out. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">A European social model</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Obviously, membership in the E.U. is a big driver of success here. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you go back to the origins of the Russia-Ukraine war, a big issue is that for all its many flaws, the E.U. has been a growth platform for the countries of Central and Eastern Europe. An independent Ukraine naturally wants in on that, which would mean falling out of the Russian sphere of influence. Russia, by contrast, wants to keep Ukraine in its sphere of influence, which denies the country its best chance at economic development. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Poland is also “European” for the purposes of American political arguments. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/642d5041-85fe-483c-b6f7-3935e7703683?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">minimum wage</a><span>, for example, is over 50 percent of the national average wage and more like two-thirds of the national median. Going off the average, this would be something like an $18/hour minimum wage in the U.S. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Poland has a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b8e8b77f-15be-4466-96ba-24a01e145221?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">national health-insurance fund called NFZ</a><span> that offers universal coverage, which can be supplemented by paying out of pocket for private clinics or purchasing private add-on insurance. This is not “Medicare for All” as defined by American progressives, who are modeling their proposal on Canada’s Medicare system, which works hard to restrict private health care. It’s more like Medicare, the actual American public health-insurance program for seniors, which has always been supplemented by private care. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In Poland, they have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/efc346a7-eeea-416d-b436-0eb304141bc4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">2.5 guns per hundred people</a><span> — much lower than France or Germany (19.6 per hundred each) to say nothing of the U.S., where we have more guns than people. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Warsaw has a two-line metro system, with plans in the works to build three more lines. This is in a metro area of about 3.2 million people, similar to Tampa or San Diego.</p><table class="twitter-embed tweet" role="presentation" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" But along with nice old buildings (which Poland has some of, though fewer than most European countries due to wartime destruction), I think these are the main sources of progressives’ Europe envy. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Actual European public policy is more complicated than this. In France and many other continental countries, for example, there is a requirement for rich people to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/97933d8d-0513-483a-a88a-9072574396f4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">give a minimum amount of inheritance to their kids when they die</a><span>. You can’t leave 70 percent of your fortune to charity and divide 30 percent among your two kids — they each get 25 percent minimum. That’s nuts! But it’s not for the sake of such policies that American progressives feel compelled to defend Europe’s honor. </span></p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Tech start-ups are good</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be clear, despite 30 years of rapid economic growth, Poland is still </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3871e4de-2640-402d-9f68-ee86c9014e62?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">poorer than Italy or France</a><span>, to say nothing of the U.S. It’s not like they’ve solved all their problems. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Poland has prospered thanks primarily to foreign direct investment dragging the country’s manufacturing sector up closer and closer to German standards. But I do think some of its more “European” aspects have been helpful here. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The high minimum wage, for example, helps ensure that even though the export sector is a minority of the workforce, upward pressure on wages from successful export jobs leads to higher pay across the board. You could imagine a world in which the Polish economy was much more segmented, with foreign investment driving higher pay for a few without directly benefiting most Polish people. That could set the stage for backlash against the investment or efforts to expropriate it or other problems. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Still, you can’t get richer than Germany just by having German companies open factories in your country. Eventually, Poland will want to have what the U.S. has: companies operating on the global technological frontier. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That’s hard to pull off. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a genuine achievement of American economic policy that we have so many of these companies. Realistically, we probably also got a bit lucky. The benefits of those companies being present in the U.S. — or, really, in the San Francisco Bay Area and Seattle specifically — have been smaller than they ought to have been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ac589575-ae20-4d7d-8c83-559bc5a1c39a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">thanks to constrained housing supply</a><span>. But when thinking about what Poland or any other European country could do to foster more high tech, it’s important to avoid hazy generalizations and think specifically. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s clearly not the case that better mass transit infrastructure would kill tech start-ups. Would stricter gun regulation? Of course not. How about if we had higher payroll taxes and public sector provision of health insurance? Again, no. If anything, that would make life easier for start-ups. And it would have zero implications whatsoever for founders or investment in high-growth start-ups. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Europe’s problems in this regard almost certainly relate to the nitty-gritty of actually launching a new business quickly and — most of all — the fact that it’s very costly to lay workers off in Europe, which makes it hard to hire or engage in rapid growth. We should not copy those specific aspects of the European social model. Note, though, that California, where most of the successful start-ups are, already has a very high top income-tax rate. For better or worse, that’s not stopping them from having a successful tech sector. But non-tax aspects of the European regulatory system do seem to be making things harder over there. </p><p class="button-wrapper" 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">Dear readers,</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In 2017, John Fetterman, then the mayor of Braddock, Pennsylvania (population 1,721), was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. This is a serious but common cardiac condition that raises the risk of stroke and can be effectively treated with medication and lifestyle modifications. Fetterman did respond to this diagnosis by losing weight but he didn’t follow up with his cardiologist or take prescribed medication, and five years later he had a stroke that nearly killed him, just a few days before winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Graham Platner doesn’t work for a living. As </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9544d4dd-9393-47ac-b18f-91b9a8eeb006?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The New York Times</a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9544d4dd-9393-47ac-b18f-91b9a8eeb006?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> reports</a><span>, the bulk of his income comes from a military disability pension of approximately $60,000 a year. The pension doesn’t mean he’s too disabled to work — he is, after all, currently seeking the job of U.S. Senator — but his recent non-campaign endeavors seem more like hobbies than a career. He runs an oyster farm that principally sells oysters to his mother’s restaurant. He earned a small stipend as his town’s harbor master: $3,000 last year. He lives in a $205,000 house that he bought with a $200,000 loan from his father.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Fetterman, like Platner, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8037b1d7-d36a-40e9-8ed3-ba64c5b54905?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">remained financially dependent on his parents into his 40s</a><span>, until he reached a high elected office that paid a meaningful salary: lieutenant governor.</span><strong> </strong><span>People complain about ‘nepo babies,’ but do you know what’s worse than a nepo baby? Someone who grows up with the advantage of privileged birth but is too mediocre or lazy to parlay that advantage into professional success, instead flailing underemployed through middle age on the parental dime until he is somehow rescued from his failure to launch by getting elected to public office. That’s the Fetterman-Platner model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Platner famously got a tattoo of a somewhat obscure Nazi symbol while he was in the Marines, drunk on shore leave in Croatia. I believe his claim that</span><strong> </strong><span>he didn’t know what the symbol meant when he got the tattoo. I </span><em>don’t</em><span> believe he didn’t know what it meant until just a few months ago when he decided to run for Senate and finally got it covered over. Republicans take the tattoo as a sign that Platner has Nazi sympathies, but I find that implausible too, given that his extensive and embarrassing Reddit posting history lays out a leftist political philosophy that is decidedly non-Nazi.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">No, the failure to cover the tattoo indicates something different about Platner: Like John Fetterman, he is a fuckup.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These men lack conscientiousness, meaning they don’t take care of the things they should take care of, whether that’s staying on blood thinners, covering up a Nazi tattoo, or getting a job. They are messy and immature, and they make gobsmackingly stupid choices as a result. Platner isn’t </span><em>just</em><span> the kind of guy who uses Kik to sext with women who are</span><strong> </strong><span>not his wife — he’s the kind of guy who, after his Kik sexting is discovered during his campaign’s self-opposition research, </span><em>fails to delete his Kik account before the press finds his profile picture in which he’s shirtless and strategically holding his phone to obscure his Nazi tattoo. </em><span>(</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c76b90e3-0cd4-4035-8bfe-9bcd442ea51b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Apparently, he still hasn’t deleted it</a><span>.) He’s also the kind of guy who forgets his talking points about the issue, denies claims his campaign has already admitted to, and extends the news cycle, forcing his campaign to clarify what he really meant to say.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is just a man with poor executive function overall, and geniuses in the progressive consultant class and the Maine Democratic electorate have decided to saddle us with him as a Senate candidate.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Platner’s campaign is brought to us by many of the same people who were behind Fetterman’s political rise. Rebecca Katz, who’s now advising Platner and previously was a strategist for Fetterman (and began her career working for John Edwards), says “the era of the perfect candidate is over.” Fetterman, of course, has been decidedly imperfect for the left — breaking with his party over Gaza and Iran and many of Trump’s cabinet nominees. Democrats now fear he will quit the party entirely. Many on Fetterman’s team quit working for him as he moved rightward, but the lesson of his nomination is this: if you nominate people whose life history reflects a high degree of unreliability, they may prove unreliable once in office.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But leftists have fetishized the style of the low-conscientiousness man, in some cases literally: Ken Klippenstein says voters are picking candidates like Platner as a revolt against “asexual” “smoothgroin” politicians who are presumably insufficiently horny to get on Kik and sext with strangers. Klippenstein </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ef10a2aa-c375-43f7-8889-01b1a863074d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">writes</a><span>: </span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #0025C2;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Platner’s story here is a pretty common one. This and his other “scandals” sound a lot like other former Marines I know. So when Washington acts like it’s disqualifying, what they’re really saying is that ordinary people aren’t fit for higher office.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First of all, this is unfair to ordinary people. Lots of ordinary Americans are conscientious: they honor their marital commitments, they work for a living, they don’t go on Kik if they’re over the age of 25. Even when they fail at some of these things (likelier the first two than the third), they understand that it is good and aspirational to succeed at them. And I hope at least some ordinary Americans still subscribe to the idea that our leaders should be extraordinary: a member of Congress should be better, on most measures, than the people he or she represents. I can’t be the only person who’s still interested in bourgeois virtues.</p><p class="button-wrapper" decided they prefer him over Janet Mills,</span><strong> </strong><span>Maine’s very old governor; and four years ago, Democrats in Pennsylvania decided they were much more excited by John Fetterman — what with his hoodies and baggy shorts and his extensive use of the term “jagoff” — than they were by Conor Lamb, a former Marine JAG and assistant U.S. attorney who then got elected to Congress in the Republican-leaning outskirts of Pittsburgh, helping Democrats regain the House majority. I guess Lamb is a “smoothgroin” because he has been consistently employed since college? Back in 2022, leftists seemed to think he was a suspiciously establishment figure, unlike the committedly progressive, anti-establishment Fetterman. But I’ll tell you one thing: If Lamb were in the Senate right now, I don’t think he would have cast the deciding vote that made Markwayne Mullin Homeland Security Secretary.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Klippenstein says Americans are tired of “clean-cut types who’ve harbored ambitions for political office since they were on high school student council and have lived every waking moment accordingly,” but one virtue of the consistently-striving Tracy Flick archetype is that these people are </span><em>consistent</em><span>. They’ve had a plan since they climbed out of the womb and that helps us know what they will do if they get into office. Leftists have turned “McKinsey” into an epithet, but getting a job at McKinsey is damned hard. My college GPA wasn’t high enough to get hired there. Having worked there is a signal that you work hard, you complete your assignments, you adapt well to new tasks and requirements, and you’re ready to take on new challenges. Is that so bad? We </span><em>don’t</em><span> </span><em>want</em><span> politicians who are full of surprises. We want ones who set clear goals and then achieve them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>If</em><span> nothing seriously more embarrassing and damaging comes out, Platner will be able to win a general election in Maine. He is running in a state with a strong Democratic lean and this is going to be a strong Democratic year. Jay Jones, another similarly “imperfect” candidate, managed to get elected attorney general of Virginia last year despite </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f127954c-f434-4f5b-b293-90d39e9f07b4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">revelations that he was arrested for driving 46 miles an hour over the speed limit</a><span> and wished death on the children of one of his Republican colleagues. But the “if” at the start of this paragraph is a big “if.”</span><strong> </strong><span>I lack confidence that Platner won’t be further damaged by much more embarrassing stories to come.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Even if he does win, I believe that, as with Fetterman, his unreliable nature — his manifest lack of conscientiousness — will come back to bite Democrats in the ass once he serves in the Senate. Most of all, it is likely to</span><strong> </strong><span>haunt the progressives who poured their hopes and dreams into his “imperfect” vessel, as they did with John Fetterman’s vessel before. As for moderates like me, I am less sure. His unreliability means he might break my way on policy. But then, he might not; Fetterman hasn’t exactly moderated in ways</span><em> </em><span>I</span><em> </em><span>find appealing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In either case, this whole misadventure is destined to end more poorly than if Democrats had found a normal candidate under the age of 60 to run in Maine. And once that becomes clear to everyone, I hope the progressive left will learn the lesson they have obstinately failed to learn from the Fetterman episode.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Very seriously,</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Josh</p><div class="subscription-widget-wrap"
